newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: KOREAN AIR INSURED PASSENGERS FOR ABOUT $134,000.
newsitem.headline: KOREAN AIR INSURED PASSENGERS FOR ABOUT $134,000.

text.p: Korean Air Lines (KAL) carried liability insurance equivalent to $134,000 for each passenger aboard the jet that crashed on the Pacific island of Guam, a company executive said on Thursday.
KAL vice president Lee Tae-won told reporters the airliner's liability coverage, denominated in special drawing rights (SDRs), amounted to 100,000 SDRs per passenger.
The value of SDRs is based on a currency basket with specific weightings of major traded currencies. One SDR was quoted at $1.34 on Thursday.
Lee said the insurance payment would cover compensation for injury or death, medical treatment and funeral costs.
Kim Young-ki, deputy general manager at KAL's legal department, said the sum is the maximum compensation per passenger under the airliner's own regulation.
The liability coverage is in line with European airliners, while the U.S. Department of Transportation recommends 250,000 SDRs. This compares with $75,000 required under the 1929 Warsaw Convention.
The world airline industry has been in discussions about updating the liability limit as the Warsaw Convention was viewed as too old and outdated, but nothing has been finalised yet.
KAL's liability coverage would protect the company from lawsuits from victims' family members, Kim said.
But the payment for an individual victim would vary in accordance with injuries and lost income.
KAL Flight 801 with 254 people on board crashed early on Wednesday on Guam. By the latest count, 27 people survived.
Industry analysts said KAL also would make special compensations, making payments an average of 200 million won ($224,000) per victim.

The company paid additional compensation to victims of a KAL DC-10 jet, which crashed in 1989 near fog-bound Tripoli airport. About 80 passengers were killed and 70 were injured in the incident, which was blamed on the pilot.
The amount of the additional compensation in that disaster was not immediately available.
But the airliners' liability would be unlimited if the crash was found to be the result of wilful misconduct.
"As there is no wilful misconduct for the crash, KAL's liability is limited," Kim said.
The cause of the Guam crash has not been determined.
Korean Air had filed an insurance certificate with the U.S. Department of Transportation to meet the country's minimum liability coverage requirement of at least 250,000 SDRs per person.
Guam is a U.S. territory.
However, Korean Air would not be required to pay anything above the 100,000 SDRs unless misconduct were found.
Lee also said the crashed Boeing 747-300 jet itself was insured for $60 million, the market value of an aircraft similar to the downed 13-year-old jet.
He said Oriental Fire and Marine Insurance would cover 0.81 percent of the insurance payment with Lloyd's of London covering the remainder.
"At present, Korean Air is in consultation with Lloyd's to work out the problems related to insurance," a KAL statement said.
An Oriental Fire official declined comment. "It's a private deal with our customer so we cannot reveal it," he said.
Both Oriental Fire and KAL are affiliates of South Korea's transportation conglomerate Hanjin Group HANJ.CN.

"An estimated $100 million is expected to be paid by insurers to Korean Air. Insurers will raise KAL's premium when the contract is renewed to offset their losses," said a senior official at a Korean re-insurance company.
KAL, which has been paying $20 million a year to insure its fleet, was expected to renew its contract in November.
"We are concerned the premium might be raised by 50 percent due to the accident," Kim said.
(Conversion $1 = 892.60 won)
